title: This is gonna completely change how people make videos in the future #shorts
description:
This is gonna completely change how people make videos in the future.

It’s called vibe directing, by OpenArt.

And this allows you to create up to 5 minute long videos just by having a conversation.

For example…this is the most ambitious video I’ve ever attempted.

It’s a scene with me eating lunch in New York City, and then out of nowhere an earthquake starts crumbling the city around me.

But as the director…when I watched this first version, it just felt like something was missing.

There’s not enough action, not enough plotline, overall I want it better.

With vibe directing, all I have to do is describe the new creative ideas in my head.

Let’s say, more buildings toppling over, the Statue of Liberty falls into the Hudson River, and I end up saving a kid with a full Ironman style rescue run.

All of those are creative ideas I can dream up, but I have no idea how to actually make them.

Now, that’s no longer a barrier.

And here’s why this finally works so well.

In addition to world class models like Seedance 2 and Nano Banana 2, the vibe director has narrative intelligence and can run the full creative process from end to end.

So as you describe what you want, it’s not just generating visuals…

It’s writing the script, building the shot plan, developing the locked-in characters and scenes, planning the color grade.

It’s a full creative team, that allows you to just be the vibe director.

This is how it’s able to generate such realistic results with this insane consistency…and it can do it for up to 5 minutes in one continuous piece.

I gotta be honest, we had so much fun making these.

And it was one of the first times where the creative process was actually as fast as my brain could imagine.

If you wanna try this out for yourself on OpenArt… 

Comment “vibe” and I’ll send you through all the different versions we made of the Earthquake scene and a full PDF with all of our best links, learnings, and prompts.
